## Same pitch, same oscillator, four different instruments

Pitch tells you which note is sounding and the oscillator supplies raw colour,
but neither one describes the gesture. A note that snaps to full level behaves
nothing like one that swells slowly into view. A long fading tail occupies
musical space in a way an abrupt stop never does. Most of what you recognise as
instrumental character lives in how amplitude changes over time.

An *envelope* splits that change into attack, decay, sustain and release. Attack
is the rise to a peak. Decay moves from that peak down toward a held level.
Sustain is the maintained portion, and release is the return to silence once the
held portion ends. Sonic Pi exposes all four as parameters, which means you can
read an envelope as data and diff two of them.

The program pins `:prophet` and C4 and plays four envelope hashes over them.
Four gestures, one pitch, one oscillator: a clipped sound, a swell, a held note,
and a note with a long tail.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 60
use_synth :prophet

envelopes = [
  {attack: 0.0, decay: 0.05, sustain: 0.1, release: 0.1},
  {attack: 1.2, decay: 0.2, sustain: 0.6, release: 0.4},
  {attack: 0.01, decay: 0.5, sustain: 1.2, release: 0.3},
  {attack: 0.02, decay: 0.2, sustain: 0.4, release: 2.0}
]

envelopes.each do |shape|
  play :c4, **shape, amp: 0.8
  sleep 3
end
```

The first envelope is over almost before it starts. The second takes more than a
whole beat to reach its peak. The third begins sharply and holds a longer body;
since the hash never lowers `sustain_level`, its decay value won't produce the
obvious drop that a lower plateau would give you. The fourth totals about 2.62
beats before any synth-specific tail, so it fills most of its three-beat slot
without spilling into the next one.

## Move one segment at a time

1. Set the slow envelope's attack to `2`. The note now spends nearly all its
   slot climbing toward the peak. Here's the interesting part: when do you think
   the note *arrived*? It won't be when the code triggered it.

2. Restore the original and raise the percussive envelope's release from `0.1`
   to `1.5`. The attack is untouched, so the onset lands in exactly the same
   place, but the tail now fills what used to be silence. You've changed
   connection without moving a single onset.

3. Restore the envelopes and add `sustain_level: 0.2` to the held shape. Now
   listen to the decay from the initial peak. A lower plateau is what makes that
   internal drop audible at all.

Hold pitch, synth and the other segments fixed through each edit. Attack,
release and sustain level each expose a different part of the note's history.

## An envelope is a state machine

It moves from silence to peak, from peak to a sustained level, and from that
level back to silence. These are phases of one gesture, not four independent
effects. Change the attack and you change where the listener locates the
beginning. Change the release and you change how the note gives up its space.

Scheduling and envelope time stay separate, and confusing them will cost you
hours later. `sleep 3` decides when the *next* event triggers. It has no power
to make the current sound stop. A release longer than the sleep will overlap the
next note; a short envelope leaves silence before the next trigger. That
distinction becomes essential in Part 3, where you'll need to tell an absent
attack apart from a tail still fading through a rest.

Because the four hashes are data, you can compare their attack values, sort them
by release, or copy one profile onto another pitch without rendering anything.
Playback supplies what the data can't: synths have their own response curves,
and extreme settings won't sound proportional to their numbers. Compare envelope
shapes on one synth before assuming another behaves the same way.

Words like staccato, legato and accent all draw on these same variables. A
detached note usually pairs a clear attack with a short sounding body. A
connected line overlaps releases across successive onsets. An accent can involve
amplitude, attack, or both at once. The vocabulary gets much more useful once
you can hear which segment is carrying the effect.

Part 2 sets timbre aside and organises pitches into a twelve-class cycle. The
envelope doesn't go anywhere. It comes back the moment those pitches need
clearer separation or a different kind of connection.

## Take it further

Pick a short recorded sound on your computer and listen past its pitch to its
amplitude shape. Is the attack immediate or gradual? Does the level fall after
the peak, and is there a body left afterwards? How does it get back to silence?
Encode your estimate as a fifth envelope hash and alternate it against the four
references.

You're after a recognisable gesture, not an imitation of the recording's timbre.
Write down which segment controls each audible difference, and note anything the
four-stage model simply can't express. Then audition it in Sonic Pi 5. Valid
Ruby establishes the shape of your data and tells you nothing whatsoever about
the synth's actual response curve.
